newsitem.title: USA: Coffee gains on stocks, heating oil surges.
newsitem.headline: Coffee gains on stocks, heating oil surges.

text.p: Coffee and heating oil futures prices surged Thursday amid mounting concern about supplies.

Cattle prices fell sharply at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange on forecasts cash prices have peaked, while cocoa prices tumbled on technical selling as traders wait production data from Europe and Ivory Coast.

Coffee prices continued a surge that began Monday when the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange reported that stocks in warehouses that qualify for delivery of futures contracts had reached a 10-year low.

"There is a real tightness is the physical market," said Victor Henriquez, president of trading firm Hencorp Becstone. "You don't see any coffee coming in yet from Central America...and roasters need to start buying as the weather turns colder and demand picks up."
December coffee futures rose 2.05 cents to 107.45 cents, after posting a high of 107.70.

Heating oil rose to the highest level since the Gulf War as the onset of cool autumn weather exacerbated fears of supply shortages this winter. Industry reports showed heating oil inventories are low.
"Heating oil doesn't want to give up. They're going to push it all the way to 80 cents," said one New York-based trader, noting such levels are unusual for this time of year.
"Basically, the sky's the limit," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst at ING Derivatives in New York. "It's low stocks, cold weather, and it's technical strength."

According to American Petroleum Institute (API) data, heating oil stocks on the East Coast, the largest heating oil market in the world stood at 23.7 million barrels at the end of last week, or just over half their year-ago levels.
NYMEX November heating oil settled 2.71 cents higher at 74.69 cents. November crude oil was up 0.76 cent at $24.81 per barrel and November gasoline was up 1.26 cents at 63.68 cents per gallon.
Cattle prices tumbled as traders believed recent gains in cash markets have run their course and prices will move lower.
Also, since late Wednesday two meat packers announced cutbacks in beef production becaue of losses on beef sales, which may lessen demand for cattle.
As a result, CME December live cattle closed down the 1.50-cent-per-lb daily limit at 66.3 cents. October closed down 1.375 cents at 72.125.
Cocoa at New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa exchange posted losses for the fourth consecutive session, sinking to one-month lows largely on speculative traders exiting long positions.
Cocoa's December contract fell $15 a tonne to $1,342, its lowest settlement since September 3.
One analyst noted the cocoa market's technical stance appeared weak and said the December contract may fall to its contract low of $1,290.
Fundamentally, traders await European cocoa production data expected late this week. Traders also await Ivory Coast crop data, due October 15, to better gauge the size of this year's harvest.
"Certainly everyone will agree the crop is not as good as last year's. The big question is by how much," he added.
